title: Application Security
description: Security at scale: CVE triage, upgrade strategy, build rules, SAST, safe errors and security review.
resumo: Triage by reachability, scope and active exploitation (KEV, EPSS) — not only CVSS.
Suppressions always have a reason and an expiry date.
Upgrade small and often, one library or group per PR; OpenRewrite for big migrations.
Maven Enforcer bans vulnerable versions and catches conflicts — adopt it in steps on legacy projects.
SAST finds dangerous patterns in your code; suppress one finding at a time, with a justification.
Generic 500s with an error id; the same login error for unknown user and wrong password.
Review security in context: access per resource, input sinks, DTOs, logs, secrets, dependencies — beyond the diff.

subsections.subtitle: CVE Triage
subsections.description: Prioritizing alerts with judgment, not only the score.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the scanner reports 60 CVEs. Fixing them all today is impossible, and ignoring them is not an option.

**Concept:** CVSS measures the generic severity of a flaw, not the risk to your application. In triage, ask: is the vulnerable part used (the CVE is in the YAML parser, but the application never reads YAML from outside)? Is the library in the production classpath, or only in tests (`test` scope)? Is it being exploited — CISA's KEV catalog lists actively exploited CVEs, and EPSS estimates the probability of exploitation? A false positive (the scanner confused the library with another) can be suppressed, always with a written justification and a review date.

**How it works:** the outcome of triage is a decision per CVE — fix now, schedule, or suppress with a reason — recorded where the team can see it.
examples.code:
<!-- dependency-check-suppressions.xml -->
<suppressions xmlns="https://jeremylong.github.io/DependencyCheck/dependency-suppression.1.3.xsd">
  <suppress until="2027-06-30Z">
    <notes>False positive: the CPE confuses the client library with the server of the same name.
    Reviewed in PR #123.</notes>
    <packageUrl regex="true">^pkg:maven/com\.example/http-client@.*$</packageUrl>
    <cve>CVE-2024-12345</cve>
  </suppress>
</suppressions>

<!-- pom.xml -->
<configuration>
  <suppressionFile>dependency-check-suppressions.xml</suppressionFile>
</configuration>
examples.interview_question: A critical CVE appeared, but the vulnerable function is not used by the application. What do you do?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A suppression with no expiry date and no reason. It becomes a permanent blind spot: a year later the code changes, the vulnerable function is now used, and the alert never comes back.
examples.code:
<!-- WRONG: no notes, no until -->
<suppress>
  <cve>CVE-2024-12345</cve>
</suppress>

<!-- RIGHT: why, where it was reviewed, and when to look again -->
<suppress until="2027-06-30Z">
  <notes>Not reachable: we never parse external YAML. Reviewed in PR #123.</notes>
  <cve>CVE-2024-12345</cve>
</suppress>

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the project has not upgraded anything in two years; now a critical CVE needs a new major version, and the upgrade takes a month.

**Concept:** the longer a dependency stays still, the harder it is to upgrade: several major versions pile up breaking changes. Small, frequent upgrades are cheaper. For each one: read the release notes and migration guide looking for breaking changes; upgrade one library (or one coherent group, such as all of Jackson) per pull request; run unit, integration and API tests; and compare `dependency:tree` before and after to see what changed along with it.

**How it works:** large migrations, such as Spring Boot 2 to 3 (`javax` to `jakarta`), deserve their own task and tools like OpenRewrite, which applies the changes automatically.
examples.code:
# Before and after the upgrade
mvn dependency:tree > tree-before.txt
# ... update the pom.xml ...
mvn dependency:tree > tree-after.txt
diff tree-before.txt tree-after.txt

# Available updates, ignoring unstable versions
mvn versions:display-dependency-updates \
  -Dmaven.version.ignore='.*-(alpha|beta|rc|M)\d*'

# Automatic Spring Boot 2 -> 3 migration with OpenRewrite
mvn -U org.openrewrite.maven:rewrite-maven-plugin:run \
  -Drewrite.recipeArtifactCoordinates=org.openrewrite.recipe:rewrite-spring:RELEASE \
  -Drewrite.activeRecipes=org.openrewrite.java.spring.boot3.UpgradeSpringBoot_3_0
examples.interview_question: How do you reduce the risk of breaking the application when upgrading a dependency?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A big-bang upgrade: every dependency at once, in one pull request. When something breaks, nobody knows which upgrade caused it, and the whole change is reverted — CVE fixes included.
examples.code:
WRONG: "chore: upgrade all dependencies" — 34 libraries, 2 majors
         -> a test fails -> revert everything

RIGHT: one PR per library or group, weekly (Dependabot or Renovate)
         -> a failure points at one upgrade

subsections.subtitle: Build Rules with Maven Enforcer
subsections.formerSubtitle: Regras no Build com Maven Enforcer
subsections.description: The build fails before the wrong version gets in.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a CVE was fixed by forcing a version; months later, an unrelated upgrade brings the vulnerable version back, and nobody notices.

**Concept:** the Maven Enforcer Plugin checks rules on every build. `bannedDependencies` forbids known vulnerable versions, even when they arrive as transitive dependencies; `dependencyConvergence` fails when two libraries ask for different versions of the same dependency — a conflict that can cause `NoSuchMethodError` in production; `requireUpperBoundDeps` makes sure the version chosen is not lower than one that is requested.

**How it works:** a fix then cannot be undone by accident in a future upgrade.
examples.interview_question: How do you stop a vulnerable library version from coming back in a future upgrade?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Turning on `dependencyConvergence` in a large project in one go. It reports dozens of conflicts, the build is red for everyone, and the rule gets removed. Start with `requireUpperBoundDeps` and `bannedDependencies`, fix conflicts with `dependencyManagement`, and enable convergence once it passes.
examples.code:
# WRONG: added to a 5-year-old project on a Friday
[ERROR] Rule 0: DependencyConvergence failed ... (47 conflicts)

# RIGHT: in steps
1. bannedDependencies + requireUpperBoundDeps
2. pin the conflicting versions in <dependencyManagement>
3. then <dependencyConvergence/>

subsections.subtitle: Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
subsections.description: Finding dangerous patterns in your own code.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** dependency scanners check the libraries, but the SQL built by concatenation is in your own code.

**Concept:** SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyzes your source or bytecode without running it. SpotBugs with the Find Security Bugs plugin detects SQL built by concatenation, weak cryptography and unsafe deserialization. Semgrep, CodeQL and SonarQube do the same with their own rules. SAST produces false positives, so a person has to read the results.

**How it works:** running it in CI on every pull request finds a problem while it is still cheap to fix.
examples.code:
<plugin>
  <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
  <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>4.8.6.6</version>
  <configuration>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>com.h3xstream.findsecbugs</groupId>
        <artifactId>findsecbugs-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>1.13.0</version>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

# Run, and fail on findings
mvn spotbugs:check

# A typical finding
[ERROR] SQL_INJECTION_JDBC: This use of java/sql/Statement.executeQuery
        can be vulnerable to SQL injection [CustomerDao.java:42]
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between dependency scanning and SAST?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Silencing findings in bulk to make the build pass. A package-wide exclusion hides the false positives and every real issue that appears there later. Suppress one finding at a time, with a justification.
examples.code:
<!-- WRONG: the whole package ignored -->
<Match><Package name="~com\.shop\..*"/></Match>

// RIGHT: one finding, one reason
@SuppressFBWarnings(value = "SQL_INJECTION_JDBC",
    justification = "column name comes from the SORTABLE allowlist")

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an unhandled exception returns the database message to the client — table names, the SQL — information that helps an attacker build an injection.

**Concept:** centralize error handling in a `@RestControllerAdvice`: known exceptions become clear responses (404, 400), and anything else becomes a generic 500 with an id that links the response to the internal log, where the details stay. `ProblemDetail` (RFC 9457) standardizes the format.

**How it works:** the error id lets support find the exact log entry without exposing anything to the client.
examples.interview_question: Why should an API not return the original message of a database exception to the client?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Different messages for "user not found" and "wrong password" at login. An attacker learns which emails have accounts (user enumeration) and focuses on them. Return the same message and status for both.

subsections.subtitle: Security-Focused Code Review
subsections.formerSubtitle: Revisão de Código com Foco em Segurança
subsections.description: What to look for in a pull request beyond the logic.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every tool passed, and the pull request still exposes another customer's orders.

**Concept:** tools catch known patterns; review catches what depends on context. The points that pay off most: access control per resource (may this user see this order, not just "is logged in"?); external input reaching SQL, file paths, URLs or commands; new fields in response DTOs; personal data in logs; secrets in code or configuration files; and new or upgraded dependencies (are they needed, is the version the fixed one?). When reviewing a 3PP upgrade, check that the cited CVE is really fixed in the chosen version.

**How it works:** keep a checklist in the pull request template, so the questions are asked every time.
examples.code:
Security checklist for a PR:
[ ] New endpoints check permission on the resource, not only authentication
[ ] No query builds SQL/JPQL by concatenating external input
[ ] Response DTOs gained no sensitive fields
[ ] New logs do not record passwords, tokens or personal data
[ ] No secret in code, tests or application.properties
[ ] New dependencies are needed and have no known CVE
[ ] 3PP upgrade: the new version fixes the cited CVE (check the advisory)
examples.interview_question: When reviewing a pull request, what do you check from a security point of view?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Reviewing only the lines in the diff. A new endpoint can look perfect and still be public, because its path falls under an existing `permitAll()` rule in a file the PR did not touch. Check how new code fits the configuration around it.
